s13.slug: SATURDAY · 12:15 AM · EL PASO — THE GLOVEBOX
body: The chart taped to the dash is a seating chart. It knows where everybody’s knees go, and it has nothing to say about who drives. For that there is the glovebox. Kevin is in the passenger seat with the door open and the dome light on and the glovebox down on its hinge against his shins, and he unfolds the second sheet along creases that have been in it since the Anacapa lot, and smooths it flat on his clipboard, and holds it up into the light.

body.title: The glovebox
body.text: DRIVERS. KEVIN — MARISOL → AZ LINE. THEO — AZ LINE → PICACHO (KEVIN RIDES SHOTGUN). MARGOT — PICACHO → EL PASO. JACK — EL PASO → FORT STOCKTON. NAVIGATOR — LENA. KEVIN — FORT STOCKTON → SAN ANTONIO. THEO — SAN ANTONIO → LAFAYETTE. KEVIN — LAFAYETTE → DUPRE ST. LANEY — NO. (UNANIMOUS.) · In the margin, small, in the same capitals: RESPECTFULLY — K.

body: Jack reads it from the driver’s door with the keys in his fist, still warm from Margot’s hand. His own name, and El Paso, and Fort Stockton, a place he has never heard of and is now responsible for. Down in the margin by the fold, smaller than the rest, is something that isn’t a driver.
“Respectfully what?”
Kevin folds the sheet in half along its crease. “It’s a chart,” he says. “The chart is the chart.”

In the way-back Theo is up on one elbow, with a hand on the lump under the blanket that is Laney. “Price. Price. There’s a navigator position open.” The lump does not open. From under the beanie, from a long way down: “I will end you.” The beanie goes lower.
“Kevin,” Theo says. “I’ll navigate —”
“You drive at San Antonio,” Kevin says. “Sleep. That’s medical.”
Theo opens his mouth, and looks at the folded sheet in Kevin’s hand, and shuts it. He lies back down in the corner of the way-back with his camel coat pulled up to his chin, and shuts his eyes.

Lena has been standing by the side door all this while with the legal pad against her chest. She leans in past Kevin’s shoulder and reads the sheet where he’s holding it to the light, all of it, down to the margin. She doesn’t say anything. She reaches back into the way-back, takes the slip out of the door pocket where Theo left it, and puts it under the clip with the others. She takes the road atlas out of the pocket on the back of the passenger seat, Kevin’s mother’s Rand McNally with a church bulletin marking Arizona, and gets into the passenger seat, because the sheet says LENA.

Kevin climbs into the middle row, into Jack’s chair, and gets a plastic rosary out of the pocket of his quarter-zip. Margot is already asleep across the aisle from him, sitting bolt upright with her arms crossed over her printed maps, her glasses still on.

Jack gets in behind the wheel. Margot left the seat run up to the dash, and the wheel is in his ribs and his knees are at the dash. He drops the seat back a notch at a time on its lever until he can breathe. Across the console Lena has the atlas open on her knees and her face to her window, and the dome light goes out on its own, slowly, and leaves the dash.

choices.text: *Fix the mirrors so you can see the road and nothing else.*
response: He works the little switch on his door. The left mirror comes down onto the lane. The right one swings out past her window, and she lets it, and doesn’t turn her head. The rearview he tips up with one finger until it holds the back window and the lot behind them, the canopy and the pumps, and not one face.
He takes the van out past the air pump and up the on-ramp, and the 10 takes them, and El Paso goes back over his shoulder in orange, and ahead of the headlights there isn’t anything at all.

choices.text: *A Hail Mary for the road, under your breath, the way Pop does at the on-ramp.*
response: Pop says it every time, at the bottom of the ramp onto 680 with the Silverado in second, the same speed he says grace. Jack says it at the bottom of this one, under the engine, *Hail Mary, full of grace*, straight through to the *Amen*. Whether the passenger seat hears it, he doesn’t look to see.

The ramp lifts them up out of the lights and sets them down on the 10, and El Paso thins out behind them, a billboard, a dealership, a last cluster of yard lights, and then there is only the road and what the headlights can find of it.

— and he stops, because Kevin is behind him in the middle row with his eyes shut and the plastic beads going through his fingers, already into the first decade, lips moving. There’s nobody to tell it to but her. She turns a page of the atlas to a map that is mostly brown and has one red line across it. He doesn’t finish.
He puts the van in drive. The on-ramp carries them up out of the lights and onto the 10, east, and the dark comes up to meet the windshield and stays out there in front of them.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 3:00 AM · I-10 EAST, CULBERSON COUNTY — QUARTER TANK
body: Culberson County is dark in every direction but forward. The headlights go out ahead a little way and give up, and past where they give up there is no house, no yard light, no glow over a rise where a town might be. Now and then something comes up out of the east, a knot of amber running lights that hangs on the horizon a long time before it turns into a truck, and goes by in a slam of air that rocks the van on its springs, and then the dark closes up behind it. On the left a long black edge cuts off the bottom of the stars. Mountains. The Sierra Diablo, if the atlas on her knees has it right.

Back at Sierra Blanca the Border Patrol had the eastbound lanes funneled down under lights like a high-school ballpark’s, and an agent in a green jacket walked a flashlight down the side of the van across six faces, four of them asleep, and leaned to the window. “Y’all U.S. citizens?” “Yes, sir,” Jack said, for all six. The flashlight rested on Laney’s beanie and moved on, and the agent stepped back and waved them through.

Since then the radio has been on scan, turned down low enough that it is mostly hiss: static, and static, and a man talking fast in Spanish over an accordion, and gone, and static again, the numbers on the display turning over and over and finding nothing they want to keep.
The clock on the dash says 2:00. Kevin set it with his thumbnail at the Colorado River and nobody has touched it since, and somewhere back in the dark the van went out of the time it’s keeping.

Jack drives. The speedometer needle sits on sixty-five, where Kevin’s card says it lives. His eyes are full of grit. His hands stopped shaking a long way back, in El Paso, and since then there has been the white line coming at him out of the dark, dash and dash and dash, and the reflectors on their posts, and the trucks, and he has not had to think about anything that wasn’t one of those.

In the passenger seat Lena is a shape with its hood up. She has her Keds on the edge of the seat and her arms around her shins and the atlas open on top of her knees, and she has been facing her window since the on-ramp. Kevin’s card is still taped to the dash at four corners, just above her knee, in the block capitals: SPEED: 65. NOT 66. OIL AT THE AZ LINE. GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER. RECEIPTS TO LENA.
Six miles short of Van Horn, without turning her head from the glass, she says it.
“Quarter tank.”
Her voice is rough from not being used. He looks down. The needle on the gas gauge is sitting on the quarter mark, exactly where the card says it must never be allowed to go.

choices.text: “Van Horn’s six miles. I’ll get it.”
choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said you’d get it.
response: “Okay.”

A green sign comes up into the headlights, VAN HORN, and then the exit. He puts the blinker on, though there is nobody on the road to tell, and the blinker going is loud in the van, and he takes the ramp down toward the only lit thing for fifty miles.

choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said Kevin was going to have you killed. She said he’d want it in writing.
response: “He’ll want it in writing.”

Something comes out of his nose that is most of the way to a laugh. In the middle row Kevin, asleep, says a word that might be *gauge* and turns his face into the headrest. The exit for Van Horn comes up green in the lights, and Jack takes it, slow, and the van rolls down the ramp toward a white canopy standing out by itself on the dark.

choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said you didn’t see it. She said she knew; you were looking at the road.
response: “I know,” she says. “You were looking at the road.”

She pulls the atlas up off her knees and holds it to the dash light, and puts a finger on a dot, and puts the atlas back. The exit comes. He takes it, and they go down the ramp into Van Horn: a canopy, and a store, and a lot of dark around both.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 3:10 AM · VAN HORN → KENT — ANYTHING BUT THE THING
body: Under the canopy the light comes straight down, white, onto the concrete and the pumps and the two of them, and when Jack opens his door the cold comes in after him and goes for the back of his neck. It’s the high desert in February. His breath goes up in the light. The pump handle is cold enough to hurt, and the card reader takes his card on the second swipe.
Lena gets out on her side and stands with her hands up inside her sleeves, and tips her head back.

He looks up too. He has never seen this many. Youngstown had the mill glow when he was little and the sodium lights after; Marisol has the fog. Here the sky comes down to the ground on every side, and there are so many of them that he can’t find the Dipper. In Ohio the Dipper was the only one there was. Through the middle of it runs a pale smear he has only ever seen in books.
She brings her head down and goes into the store. The pump runs. Out on the interstate a truck goes by without slowing, and the sound of it goes on a long time after it’s gone.
She comes back across the concrete with two coffees in lidded cups, one in each hand, and holds one out to him without a word.
“Thanks.”
“Mm.”
The pump clicks off. He tears the receipt out of the slot, and she holds out her hand for it, and it goes under the clip of the legal pad with the others.

The light leaves nothing out. Her hood is down. Her hair is flat on the side that was against the window, and there’s a red crease across her cheek from the seam of the seat, and the mascara is gone from yesterday, and the medal has worked its way out of the neck of her sweatshirt and hangs on the front of it. She blows across the hole in the lid and drinks, holding the cup up under her chin, and the steam goes up past her face.
Back on the 10 the canopy falls away behind them and the dark comes back. The coffee is too hot to drink and he drinks it.
A billboard comes up out of nothing on the right, lit from underneath: a cartoon telescope against a sky full of yellow stars, STAR PARTY, the observatory, an exit number. It goes by.
“We just had one,” he says.
She looks at it going away in her side mirror. “Theirs has a telescope.”
“Ours had coffee.”
She drinks some of hers, and doesn’t argue.
A few miles on, out of nowhere: “Seventy point six two.”
He waits.
“Brees,” she says. “Completion percentage. This season. It’s the record. In the history of the league.”
“You’ve been holding that since Van Horn.”
“I’ve been holding that since *September*.”
“Freeney’s ankle,” he says.
“It’s fine. It’s always fine.” She drinks her coffee. “Indianapolis lies about ankles.”
“Mama says Mémère called you.”
“She did.”
“Herself.”
“At seven in the morning.”
“What did she say?”
He thinks about it. “Don’t bring nothing.”

Lena laughs. It comes up out of her loud, at the windshield, a real noise in the dark van, and in the middle row Kevin’s breathing catches and goes on. “That’s her,” she says. “That’s her exactly. It means bring something.”
“I brought a pie.”
“Then you’ll live.”
“She said your father’s been sick to his stomach since the Vikings.”

“Since the *kick*. He couldn’t watch it. He went out and stood on the porch for the overtime and heard it from the porch, the street went up, and he came back in and lay down on the floor of the front room and didn’t talk for twenty minutes. Mama put a pillow under his head.” She sets the cup in the holder. “In 1980 he wore a bag on his head to the Superdome. A Schwegmann’s bag. Mama cut the eyeholes with her sewing scissors.” And her voice drops to the bottom of her chest and goes through Breaux Bridge on its way out: “‘Lord, I wore the bag for You. One and fifteen, I wore the bag. You owe me one.’”
“He says that?”
“Every day since the Vikings. Out loud. In the pew at the eight o’clock.”
“Where are we sleeping?”

“Y’all are in the attic. All three of you.” She ticks it off on her fingers in the dash light. “There’s a box fan Daddy put in the window up there in 1994, and it doesn’t turn off. It doesn’t have an off. It has loud and louder. There’s Remy’s mattress. There’s Remy’s Tiger poster. Don’t move the poster.”
“What’s behind the poster?”

“Remy’s fist, the night LSU lost to somebody he won’t say.” She takes the cup back out of the holder. “And you go up and down past Mémère. She sleeps in the front room so she can see the stairs. She’s eighty-eight. She’s never missed anybody on those stairs.”

body.text: “I owe Hale three thousand words,” he says, “on whether a Browns fan can be saved. It’s an appendix.” She drinks some coffee on it. “Saved, yes,” she says. “*Cured*, no.”

body: Kent goes by on the right, a few dark buildings and a sign, and then it’s gone too, and the road runs on east under all those stars toward a town called Balmorhea that the atlas says is there.

choices.text: *Tell her what Pop said about the Pacific.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you told Lena what your father said about the Pacific: it was big; it’s allowed.
response: He tells her about August: Pop swinging the Silverado into the first turnout on Highway 1 without a signal, the engine running and the door open and the dinger going, and walking to the guardrail with his hands in his windbreaker and standing there. Fifty-one years old, the first time. Not a word. Not in the truck, not on the phone, not for five months. “And Thursday he calls me from the garage to tell me to look at the Mississippi. And then he says, I saw the Pacific. It was big. I looked at it a while.” Jack hears his father’s voice come out of his own mouth on the next part. “It’s allowed.”
She’s quiet. Then, after a while: “That’s the best thing anybody’s ever said about an ocean.”

She lets her seat back a notch and turns in it toward the middle with her knees up. By Balmorhea the cup has gone slack in her hands, tipping, and he reaches across and takes it from her and puts it in the holder, and she doesn’t wake up.

choices.text: *The worst-season contest: the ’09 Browns against the ’80 Saints.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you and Lena argued the worst season in football, the ’09 Browns against the ’80 Saints. The Saints won by losing more.
response: “Your guys won one game,” he says. “Mine won five, and it was worse.”
“How is five *worse*?”
“Because they won the last four. Now everybody in Cleveland has hope again. That’s cruelty. Your father got to put a bag on his head and be done with it.”

“Fourteen in a row,” Lena says. “*Fourteen.* They didn’t win until December, and it was the Jets, by a point. Grown men in Schwegmann’s bags. My uncle named a dog *Aints* and the dog was ashamed.” She is up on her knee in the seat now, turned toward him, the coffee going dangerously in one hand. “Your people wear dog masks to the stadium *on purpose*.”
“That’s loyalty.”
“That’s a cry for help.” She settles back. “I win. Write it down. The Saints win by losing more.”
She puts her feet up on the dash under Kevin’s card and her arms across her chest, still winning, and by Balmorhea she is asleep like that.

choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you asked Lena what she’ll eat first. Mémère’s gumbo. Whatever her daddy boils. A cold Barq’s from the bottle.
response: She doesn’t have to think. “Mémère’s gumbo. Out of the pot, standing up, before anybody says grace, and she’ll hit my hand with the spoon. Then whatever Daddy’s boiling, and he’ll be boiling something, he’ll have been boiling since noon. Then a Barq’s.” She holds up a finger. “Cold. From the bottle. The can tastes like the can.”
“That’s three things.”

“You asked what first. That’s first.” She keeps going past first: a shrimp po’boy, dressed, the bread from Leidenheimer’s that has to crack when you press it, a king cake from somewhere he’s never heard of that she will not tell Laney about because Laney will want the baby. She lets her seat back a notch while she’s at it. Somewhere past Balmorhea she is in the middle of the bread again, and then she isn’t, and when he looks over she’s asleep with the sentence still in her mouth.

choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you let Lena talk, and listened: the house after the water, and her father and his brothers putting it back by hand.
response: He doesn’t ask her anything. He drives, and lets the road be quiet, and she fills it.

She talks about the house. Not the water: after. Daddy and his brothers took it down to the studs, every wall, and put it back up by hand, two years of Saturdays and some weeknights under a work light on an extension cord, and she held the flashlight. She was fourteen. They found cypress under the old linoleum in the front room, and Daddy got down on his knees and wouldn’t let anybody cover it up again. Her uncles sang. One of them only knew the first verse of anything. “Daddy hung every door in that house himself,” she says. “Not one of them shuts right. He says that’s how you know who did it.”

She lets her seat back a notch while she’s telling it. By Balmorhea her sentences have got farther apart, and then there isn’t another one, and when he looks over she’s asleep with her cheek against the seat back, turned toward him.

s15a.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 AM · I-10 EAST, PAST BALMORHEA — THE RIGHT ARM
s15a.music: Willie Nelson — “Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain”
body: Somewhere before Fort Stockton her head comes over the console and down onto his shoulder.

It comes the way a sleeper’s head comes, all at once and heavy, and settles, and she makes a small sound in her throat and is gone again. Her temple is on the shoulder seam of the Carhartt. Her hair has come loose from the hood, and some of it has gone into his collar, and a strand of it catches on the stubble along his jaw every time the van rides over a seam in the road. Her breath comes warm through his shirt at the collarbone, and cools, and comes warm again. The medal has swung round on its chain and lies against his sleeve, and through the canvas he can feel the small hard oval of it, and the warmth it has from her.
He drives with his left hand. His right hand is on his own knee, palm up, where it was when her head came down, and he leaves it there.

Out of the static the scan comes to a station from somewhere south of the road, and this time it holds: Willie Nelson, slow, a guitar and his voice and hardly anything else, coming in thin. When the road goes down into a low place the song goes under the hiss, and when the road comes up the other side the song is still there, a little farther off.

By the next mile marker he can feel his pulse in the shoulder she’s on. A few miles later the arm has gone to pins from the elbow down, all the way into the fingertips, and he doesn’t move it. A truck comes up behind with its brights on and pulls out and goes by, and the light runs across the inside of the van, over her face and his open hand and the cup in the holder, and away up the road, and she doesn’t wake. He is warm all down that side of him and cold down the other, where the window is. Behind him there’s only breathing: Kevin with his head against the window and the rosary gone still in his lap, Margot asleep upright with her arms crossed over her maps, two shapes in the way-back.
He drives forty miles like that, at sixty-five, with his right arm still.
Short of Fort Stockton the station goes under one last time and doesn’t come up, and he leaves the hiss where it is, low, and against his collarbone her breath goes warm, and cool, and warm.

s16.slug: SATURDAY · 5:20 AM · FORT STOCKTON — THE HANDOFF
body: Fort Stockton is a canopy, a burger sign switched off for the night on a pole over the frontage road, and the sky in the east still black. He brings the van in under the lights and puts it in park.

She wakes when it stops. She sits up and takes her head back, and pushes her hair off her face with both hands, and looks out her window at the pumps. She doesn’t say anything about it. He takes his right hand off his knee and opens and shuts it until the fingers come back to him, and he doesn’t say anything about it either.
In the rearview, in the way-back, Theo’s eyes are open. Then they aren’t.
Behind Jack, Kevin comes up out of sleep in one movement, sitting straight up in the chair with one hand already at his chest for a pen he isn’t wearing. “Where are we.”
“Fort Stockton.”

Kevin leans forward between the seats to read the gauge, well up toward F now, and then holds out his hand, palm up, to the passenger seat. Lena gives him the legal pad off her knees, receipts and clip and all, without a word. He goes through the slips under the canopy light with his lips moving, Picacho, Picacho, El Paso, Van Horn, and stops on one, and holds it up to the light like an X-ray.
“Who put ten dollars of gas in this van in El Paso.”
From the way-back, with his eyes shut: “It seemed like a lot of gasoline.”
Kevin lowers the slip. He puts it back under the clip, and smooths the clip down over it, and hands the pad back to Lena, and gets out to walk around to the driver’s door.

They change places in the cold. Kevin to the wheel, moving the seat up three notches and the mirrors back to where his mother keeps them. Margot, woken enough to be furious about it, up to the passenger seat with her printed maps against her chest. Jack back to his chair on the right. Lena to the way-back, with the atlas under her arm, past him at the side door, close in the cold, her breath going up white beside his.

response: “Mm.”
She gets a hand on the back of his chair and goes up past it into the way-back, and sits down on her side next to Laney, and puts her hood up.
She goes past him up the step into the way-back. Laney, asleep, lifts the edge of the blanket for her without waking, and Lena gets in under it and pulls her hood up.
A nod, from the way-back step, with the atlas under her arm.
